Executive Summary
This paper presents high-speed, multi-spectral observations of the lunar occultation of the carbon-rich AGB star AFGL 5440, conducted over the 1–4 µm wavelength range using the pMIRAS instrument on the McDonald Observatory 2.7-m telescope. The primary objective was to resolve the spatial structure of the circumstellar dust shell, which previous interferometric studies had not fully characterized at milli-arcsecond resolutions. The authors demonstrate that a single-size uniform disk model cannot fit the observed occultation fringes, indicating the presence of an extended dust shell. Using the DUSTY radiative transfer code, they modeled the circumstellar environment by fitting both the observed occultation light curves and the known spectral energy distribution (SED). The modeling yielded a strong constraint on the inner radius of the dust shell, corresponding to a maximum dust temperature of 950 K ± 50 K. The optical depth at 5 µm was determined to be 0.5 ± 0.1. The best-fitting models required a radial density gradient of ρ ∝ r⁻² or a gradient derived from radiatively driven hydrodynamic outflow. A significant finding is that the models could not fit the observed IRAS 60 µm flux without assuming a substantial abundance of graphite or a historically higher mass-loss rate. The derived dust mass-loss rate is 6.5 × 10⁻⁸ M⊙/yr, consistent with previous estimates but highlighting uncertainties in dust opacity. The study provides the first detailed resolution of the inner dust shell structure for AFGL 5440, constraining the recent mass-loss history and the physical location of the dust condensation front.

Research Context
Mass loss from post-main-sequence stars provides heavy elements to the interstellar medium. The mechanisms of mass loss during the AGB phase are not fully understood. Studies of spatial structure of circumstellar shells can clarify uncertainties. Molecular line studies have found periodic variations in mass-loss rates. Angular resolutions well under 1 arcsec are required to study inner regions. Lunar occultation observations have pushed angular resolutions to milli-arcsecond levels. Previous interferometric observations were typically made in one or two broad bands. The star AFGL 5440 is a carbon-rich AGB star. The distance to AFGL 5440 is estimated at 2.25 kpc. The luminosity is implied to be 1.4×10⁴ L⊙.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central question is how to resolve the dust shell around AFGL 5440. The hypothesis is that a single-size model cannot fit the occultation fringes. The study aims to model the circumstellar shell using radiative transfer. The goal is to fit both occultation light curves and the SED. It is hypothesized that the inner radius of the dust shell is constrained. The study predicts a specific dust temperature at the inner radius. The optical depth at 5 µm is expected to be constrained. The density gradient is hypothesized to follow a specific power law. The study investigates whether graphite is required to fit the IRAS flux. The mass-loss rate is expected to be derived from the model.

Methodological Details
Observations were made during an immersion occultation on 28 Aug 2001. The instrument used was pMIRAS on the McDonald Observatory 2.7-m telescope. The instrument is a high-speed spectrophotometer using a NaCl prism. The detector is a 256² InSb array. The slit width was set to about 5 arcsec. The detector read-out time was 8 msec. The spectral resolution varies from R~20 to R~100. The angular resolution is a couple milli-arcsec. Two calibration stars, IRC+00233 and HD 155292, were observed. Data reduction involved shifting images to align wavelengths. Sky subtraction was performed using the long slit. Wavelength calibration was done by fitting atmospheric transmission maxima. Flux calibration was not attempted due to variable efficiency. The modeling used the DUSTY radiative transfer code. More than 200 models were explored. Dust composition included amorphous carbon, SiC, and graphite.

Procedures And Architectures
The fringe pattern is a convolution of point source and blurring parameters. Blurring parameters include telescope aperture, integration time, and bandwidth. The source size/structure is the most important blurring parameter. A uniform disk was initially assumed as the simplest model. A χ² test was used to find the best model fit. For comparison stars, a single source size was assumed. The best fit size for IRC+00233 was 4.5 to 5.0 mas. For HD 155292, sizes less than 3 mas fit the data well. For AFGL 5440, a single size uniform disk did not fit. An 11 mas disk provided a passable fit in mid-range wavelengths. The DUSTY code was used to model the star+shell. Dust optical depth was varied to fit the energy distribution. Model source images were used to calculate expected occultation fringes. The outer radius of the dust shell was set to at least 100 times the inner radius. Grain size distributions tested included MRN and KMH shapes.

Key Results
The occultation fringes cannot be fit by any single-size model. The maximum dust temperature is constrained to 950 K ± 50 K. The optical depth at 5 µm is 0.5 ± 0.1. The best fit density gradient is ρ ∝ r⁻². Models with Tmax < 900 K did not fit the longer wavelength fringes. The inner radius of the dust shell is 3.7×10¹⁴ cm. The angular radius of the inner shell is 11 mas. The angular diameter of the central star is of order 3 mas. The dust mass-loss rate is 6.5 × 10⁻⁸ M⊙/yr. The gas mass-loss rate is 3.1×10⁻⁵ M⊙/yr. The gas-to-dust mass ratio is 600. Graphite is required to fit the IRAS 60 µm flux. Without graphite, models fail to fit the 60 µm flux by factors of 3.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The observations resolve the stellar photosphere and inner dust shell edge. The inner radius constraint implies a specific dust density gradient. The temperature constraint is below expected condensation temperatures. The need for graphite contradicts evidence against it in similar stars. The 60 µm flux may imply a recent decrease in mass-loss rate. The derived mass-loss rate is consistent with previous estimates. The study highlights uncertainties in model assumptions and dust opacities. The results support radiatively driven mass loss mechanisms. The time scale for higher past mass-loss is comparable to IRC+10216 fluctuations. The findings provide new constraints on the innermost circumstellar region.

Contradictions And Limitations
The model requires graphite, which is generally not found in such stars. The IRAS 60 µm flux cannot be fit without graphite or higher past mass-loss. The exact location of the spectrum varies due to seeing. Flux calibration was not attempted due to variable efficiency. The predicted times of occultation events can be in error by 10 seconds. The spectral resolution is lower at shorter wavelengths. The signal-to-noise ratio limits accuracy to ±2 mas. The study did not attempt to extract stellar photosphere details. The study did not thoroughly examine all dust size/composition models. The agreement with IRAS LRS data was only superficial.

Claims
The inner radius of the dust shell around AFGL 5440 is strongly constrained by the occultation data. The maximum dust temperature is 950 K ± 50 K. The inner radius is 3.7×10¹⁴ cm. The angular radius is 11 mas. This temperature is below expected condensation temperatures. This constrains the recent dust mass-loss rate.
The presence of graphite is required to fit the far-infrared flux. Models without graphite fail to fit the 60 µm flux. Graphite has a flat emissivity between 10 and 50 µm. There is evidence against substantial graphite in similar stars. This suggests a recent decrease in mass-loss rate.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
The study tested more than 200 models. Different grain size distributions (MRN, KMH) were tested. The fit quality was checked against the SED and light curves. The study compared models with and without graphite. The study compared models with different density gradients.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1 shows observed and model light curves for IRC+00233. Figure 5 shows observed light curves for AFGL 5440. Figure 7 shows the fit to the spectral energy distribution. Figure 8 shows the fit to the occultation light curves. Figure 10 illustrates the spatial profiles of the best-fit model.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is the resolution of the inner dust shell structure of AFGL 5440. 2. The strongest evidence is the constraint on the inner radius and temperature. 3. The future path involves understanding the role of graphite and mass-loss history.

summary.title: Gluon Radiation of an Expanding Color Skyrmion in the Quark-Gluon Plasma
summary.executive_summary: This paper investigates the gluon radiation emitted by an expanding color skyrmion within a quark-gluon plasma (QGP) using a semiclassical approach. The study addresses the hydrodynamic stage of deconfined hot QCD matter, specifically modeling the transport of color charges via a nonlinear sigma model. The author derives the nonabelian current corresponding to a time-dependent, expanding soliton solution, which mimics the expanding nature of the RHIC fireball. By calculating the semiclassical amplitude for gluon emission from this classical current, the paper determines the density of states and the energy spectrum of the radiation. The results reveal a distinct spectral pattern: a fast fall-off in the ultraviolet (UV) region, a smooth peak in the intermediate energy range, and a long tail in the infrared (IR) region. The IR behavior is characterized by a $1/\sqrt{k}$ dependence, which contrasts with the $1/k$ behavior found in previous literature where the medium size was assumed to be infinite. This difference is attributed to the finite soliton size $R_0$ in the current model. The work also discusses the hierarchy between medium-induced gluon radiation (jet quenching) and radiation from the medium itself, noting that the characteristic momentum of the latter is significantly smaller. The study suggests that this hydrodynamic approach could provide insights into the eccentricity of elliptic flow in relativistic heavy-ion collisions, offering a new avenue for understanding the physical mechanisms underlying particle production spectra.

documents.judge_context:
Executive Summary
This paper investigates the gluon radiation emitted by an expanding color skyrmion within a quark-gluon plasma (QGP) using a semiclassical approach. The study addresses the hydrodynamic stage of deconfined hot QCD matter, specifically modeling the transport of color charges via a nonlinear sigma model. The author derives the nonabelian current corresponding to a time-dependent, expanding soliton solution, which mimics the expanding nature of the RHIC fireball. By calculating the semiclassical amplitude for gluon emission from this classical current, the paper determines the density of states and the energy spectrum of the radiation. The results reveal a distinct spectral pattern: a fast fall-off in the ultraviolet (UV) region, a smooth peak in the intermediate energy range, and a long tail in the infrared (IR) region. The IR behavior is characterized by a $1/\sqrt{k}$ dependence, which contrasts with the $1/k$ behavior found in previous literature where the medium size was assumed to be infinite. This difference is attributed to the finite soliton size $R_0$ in the current model. The work also discusses the hierarchy between medium-induced gluon radiation (jet quenching) and radiation from the medium itself, noting that the characteristic momentum of the latter is significantly smaller. The study suggests that this hydrodynamic approach could provide insights into the eccentricity of elliptic flow in relativistic heavy-ion collisions, offering a new avenue for understanding the physical mechanisms underlying particle production spectra.

Research Context
The study addresses gluon radiation during the hydrodynamic stage of deconfined hot QCD matter. Medium-induced gluon radiation has been explored in the context of jet quenching. Spatially extended nuclear matter affects fragmentation and hadronization of hard partons. Gluon radiation is also considered in the context of gluon density saturation. The time evolution of the RHIC fireball influences observable particle production spectra. The resulting state of matter is modeled as a relativistic fluid. Generalized fluid mechanics characterizes the long-distance physics of color charge transport. A type of single skyrmion solutions in color fluid was discovered. A time-dependent skyrmion expands in time, matching the expanding fireball nature. The pattern of gluon radiation is an important character of this color skyrmion.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central question is the calculation of the gluon radiation spectrum for an expanding color skyrmion. The hypothesis is that the radiation can be calculated using a semiclassical approach. It is predicted that there is a fast fall-off in the UV side of the spectrum. A smooth peak is predicted to dominate the intermediate energy region. A long tail is predicted as the characteristic feature in the IR region. The study aims to compare these results with those in existing literatures. The model assumes a hierarchy between partonic coupling and effective coupling. Gluon self-interaction is omitted to work with a free parton picture. The lowest order semiclassical amplitude is derived from the interaction of current and field. The spatial Fourier transformation is completed analytically to simplify the amplitude.

Methodological Details
The transport of color charges is modeled by a nonlinear sigma model. The configuration of the fluid is described by a group element field U. The velocity field is defined using the trace of the group element derivative. The abelian charge current is conjugate to the velocity. The fluid takes values in an SU(2) group. The equation of state is approximated by radiation-like behavior at high temperature. The free energy density is derived by integrating the energy and pressure densities. Expanding soliton solutions are studied via variational and collective coordinate methods. The soliton size R(t) follows a specific time-dependent expansion law. The approximation is valid provided the temporal scale is much smaller than the spatial scale. A small parameter lambda is defined as the ratio of temporal to spatial scales. The hedgehog ansatz is specified for the soliton solution. The stereographic map is used to define the angle phi. The nonabelian current is derived from the abelian current via the Eckart factorization. The current is expressed in terms of the velocity and the soliton orientation. Only the lowest mode of the multipole expansion is considered in this letter. The spherically symmetric part of the current is contained in the third component. The interaction between the skyrmion and hard partons is considered. The gauge coupling becomes the coupling between a classical current and a free quantum field. The lowest order semiclassical amplitude is calculated using the Fock vacuum and one-gluon state. The gluon factor is given by the wave function with color and helicity parts. The spatial Fourier transformation is completed analytically. The time integral is evaluated using the specific form of R(t). The on-shell condition is applied to relate frequency and momentum. The radiation spectrum is given by the energy radiated over the entire time of expansion. The number distribution is calculated by summing over colors and helicities. The density of states is derived in a spherically symmetric setting. Numerical results are calculated for specific values of lambda.

Procedures And Architectures
The Lagrangian density includes terms for charge current, free energy, and gauge coupling. The velocity field is defined as the trace of the group element derivative. The energy and pressure densities are given by the ideal fluid formula. The nonabelian charge density is related to the abelian current by the Eckart factor. The free energy density is obtained by integrating the equation of state. The expanding soliton solution is given by a specific time-dependent radius function. The hedgehog ansatz is used to specify the group element field. The stereographic map defines the sine and cosine of the angle phi. The nonabelian current is derived using the equation of motion. The current has a natural form of a multipole expansion. The spherically symmetric part of the current is isolated. The semiclassical amplitude is given by the integral of the current and field. The gluon factor is the wave function of the one-gluon state. The spatial Fourier transformation is completed analytically. The time integral is evaluated using the expansion law of the soliton. The on-shell condition is used to define the parameter kappa. The final amplitude is expressed in terms of a function f_M. The number distribution is calculated by summing the squared amplitude. The density of states is derived for a spherically symmetric setting. The energy spectrum is calculated as the derivative of energy with respect to k. The numerical results are plotted for different values of lambda.

Key Results
The density of states is proportional to alpha, R0, lambda squared, and kappa to the power of negative one-half. The energy spectrum is proportional to alpha, lambda squared, kappa to the power of one-half, and the squared amplitude. The numerical results are shown for lambda equal to 1/15, 2/15, and 1/5. There is a fast fall-off in the UV side of the spectrum. A smooth peak dominates the intermediate energy region. A long tail is the characteristic feature in the IR region. The asymptotic behavior of the number density in small k is proportional to 1 over square root of k. This differs from the 1/k form found in previous literature. The difference is due to the finite medium size characterized by the soliton size R0. The IR behavior in this case is softer than in the infinite medium case. The characteristic momentum in this case is 1 over R0. The medium-induced gluon radiation frequency is significantly larger than the characteristic momentum. There is a hierarchy between the medium-induced spectrum and the medium radiation spectrum.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The pattern of gluon radiation is an important character of the color skyrmion. The hydrodynamic approach opens up possibilities to address the eccentricity of elliptic flow. This can be done intrinsically by considering the nonabelian color current. It can also be done exogenously by considering the gluon radiation patterns. Understanding the radiation pattern is important for determining physical mechanisms. The study provides a new perspective on the hydrodynamic stage of QGP evolution. The finite size of the medium affects the IR behavior of the radiation. The results suggest a distinct spectral shape compared to infinite medium approximations. The work highlights the importance of the soliton size in determining the radiation spectrum. Future work will explore the connection to elliptic flow.

summary.title: Differential recursion and differentially algebraic functions
summary.executive_summary: This paper addresses technical inaccuracies and ambiguities in Moore's definition of real-valued recursive functions, specifically focusing on the differential recursion operator. Moore originally proposed that his class of real primitive recursive functions corresponds to differentially algebraic functions, which are the functions generable by Shannon's General Purpose Analog Computer (GPAC). The author argues that Moore's original definitions lack formality regarding partial functions, leading to inconsistent claims. The paper first establishes a rigorous characterization of differentially algebraic functions, proving the equivalence of several local and global definitions involving polynomial differential equations. It then reformulates Moore's real primitive recursive functions using a mathematically sound definition of the differential recursion operator that preserves analyticity. A key contribution is the demonstration that even under this restrictive, analyticity-preserving definition, Moore's Claim 1—that real primitive recursive functions are differentially algebraic—fails. The author constructs a counterexample using a variant of Euler's gamma function, showing it is real primitive recursive but not differentially algebraic. Furthermore, the paper discusses the implications for Moore's Claim 2 regarding the relationship to standard digital recursion, noting that the inclusion of minimization operators leads to non-smooth functions, thereby breaking the connection to analog computation models. The study concludes that the purported relation between Moore's classes and analog computation fails, posing an open problem to find a subclass that maintains this relationship.

documents.judge_context:
Executive Summary
This paper presents results from the STAR collaboration on three-particle azimuthal correlations in pp, d+Au, and Au+Au collisions at a center-of-mass energy of 200 GeV. The primary objective is to investigate the presence of conical emission, specifically distinguishing between hydrodynamic Mach cone shock waves and QCD Cherenkov radiation, as mechanisms for the broadening of the away-side jet structure in heavy ion collisions. The analysis focuses on a trigger particle with transverse momentum (pT) between 3 and 4 GeV/c and two associated particles with pT between 1 and 2 GeV/c. A rigorous background subtraction method is employed, accounting for combinatorial backgrounds, hard-soft correlations, and flow harmonics (v2 and v4). The results show that while pp and d+Au collisions exhibit standard jet-like correlations with kT broadening, central Au+Au collisions display a distinct off-diagonal structure at approximately π ± 1.45 radians. This structure is consistent with conical emission. Crucially, the emission angle is found to be independent of the associated particle's pT, which supports the Mach cone hypothesis over the Cherenkov radiation model, where the angle is predicted to decrease with increasing momentum. Systematic uncertainties related to flow subtraction and normalization are investigated and found to be manageable, with the signal remaining robust under variations in these parameters. The study concludes that the observed off-diagonal peaks in central Au+Au collisions are consistent with Mach cone emission, providing evidence for hydrodynamic flow effects in the quark-gluon plasma.

Research Context
Heavy ion collisions create a medium that may be the quark gluon plasma. Two-particle jet-like azimuthal correlations show the away-side shape is broadened in central Au+Au. The away-side structure is consistent with large angle gluon radiation. It is also consistent with jets deflected by radial flow. Hydrodynamic conical flow generated by Mach-cone shock waves is a proposed mechanism. Cherenkov radiation is another proposed mechanism for the away-side structure. Three-particle correlations can differentiate conical flow from other mechanisms. The associated particle pT dependence helps distinguish conical flow from Cherenkov radiation.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The study investigates whether Mach cones exist in heavy ion collisions. It aims to distinguish conical flow from simple QCD Cherenkov radiation. The hypothesis is that conical emission produces a specific angular structure. Mach cone emission angle is expected to be independent of associated pT. Cherenkov radiation predicts an emission angle decreasing with associated pT. The analysis tests the pT dependence to discriminate between these models. Central Au+Au collisions are expected to show the strongest conical signal.

Methodological Details
Data were taken in the STAR time projection chamber. Collisions were pp, d+Au, and Au+Au at 200 GeV. Trigger particles had pT between 3 and 4 GeV/c. Associated particles had pT between 1 and 2 GeV/c. Events are treated as jet-like correlated and background particles. Hard-soft background is constructed from 2-particle jet-like correlation. Soft-soft background is obtained from mixed events. Trigger flow is added in triplet-wise from mixed events. v2 values are from reaction plane and 4-particle cumulant methods. v4 is parameterized as 1.15 times v2 squared. Background is normalized using the zero yield at one radian. The scale factor alpha corrects for multiplicity bias. The factor beta accounts for non-Poisson multiplicity distributions.

Procedures And Architectures
The 3-particle correlation analysis method is rigorously described. Raw 3-particle azimuthal distribution is shown in delta phi. Combinatorial backgrounds must be removed to obtain the signal. The hard-soft background is folded with normalized 2-particle background. The 2-particle background is constructed by mixing events. Flow modulation is added in pairwise from average v2 values. The soft-soft background includes correlations independent of the trigger. Trigger flow is accounted for in the soft-soft term. The total background includes hard-soft and soft-soft components. Normalization is performed within 0.8 to 1.2 radians. Systematic uncertainties due to subtraction and flow are investigated.

Key Results
pp and d+Au results show peaks at near-side and away-side. The away-side peak displays diagonal elongation consistent with kT broadening. Peripheral Au+Au shows additional on-diagonal elongation. Central Au+Au displays an off-diagonal structure at pi plus or minus 1.45. The off-diagonal structure increases in magnitude with centrality. The structure is prominent in the top 12% central data. Off-diagonal signals significantly deviate from zero in central Au+Au. The emission angle is consistent with constant as a function of pT. The angle is consistent with remaining constant as a function of centrality. The fit to a constant gives an angle of 1.46 radians.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The off-diagonal peaks are consistent with conical emission. The lack of pT dependence supports Mach cone emission. Cherenkov radiation predicts a decreasing angle with pT. The result is consistent with hydrodynamic conical flow. The study provides evidence for Mach cones in heavy ion collisions.

Contradictions And Limitations
Systematic uncertainties due to background subtraction are investigated. The signal is robust with respect to v2 variation. The signal is robust with respect to normalization window changes. Other sources include trigger particle flow effects. Uncertainty in v4 parameterization is a source of error. Multiplicity bias effects on soft-soft background are considered.

Claims
Central Au+Au collisions exhibit off-diagonal peaks consistent with conical emission. Off-diagonal structure is present in central Au+Au. The structure is at pi plus or minus 1.45 radians. The signal increases with centrality. pp and d+Au do not show this off-diagonal structure. This suggests the presence of conical flow in the QGP.
The emission angle is independent of associated particle pT, supporting Mach cone over Cherenkov radiation. The angle is consistent with constant as a function of pT. Cherenkov radiation predicts a decreasing angle. Systematic errors are present but do not change the conclusion. This supports the hydrodynamic Mach cone model.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
The signal is robust with respect to v2 variation. The signal is robust with respect to normalization changes. Systematic errors include trigger flow and v4 uncertainty.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1 shows raw and background-subtracted 2 and 3-particle correlations. Figure 2 shows background-subtracted 3-particle correlations for different collisions. Figure 3 shows centrality dependence of signal strengths. Figure 4 shows away-side projections for d+Au and Au+Au. Figure 5 shows emission angles as a function of pT and centrality. Figure 6 shows systematic checks for v2 and normalization.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is the observation of off-diagonal peaks in central Au+Au collisions. 2. The strongest evidence is the pT independence of the emission angle. 3. The future path is to further distinguish Mach cone from other mechanisms.

Executive Summary

The study focuses on a complex, short-range potential V(x) = Z(x) + iY(x) that satisfies PT-symmetry conditions, where Z(x) is even and real, and Y(x) is odd and real. The study concludes that the apparent asymmetry between incoming and outgoing states in PT-symmetric scattering is formal and tractable, providing a schematic model that may inform future studies on non-Hermitian inverse scattering problems.

Research Context
Standard textbooks describe stationary one-dimensional motion in real potential wells. The conventional approach has been generalized to non-Hermitian Hamiltonians. These Hamiltonians are quasi-Hermitian, Hermitian only in a metric sense. The key ideas incorporate PT-symmetry of the Hamiltonians. This development was summarized in a review by Carl Bender. The paper focuses on a simple PT-symmetric scattering model. The potential is complex, with real even and odd components. The Schrödinger equation is replaced by a Runge-Kutta-discretized version. This discretization was previously employed for bound-state problems. The study aims to fill a gap in scattering literature.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central question is how to derive reflection and transmission coefficients. The hypothesis is that a complex PT-symmetric potential allows real spectra. The study predicts that the scattering problem remains tractable. It is hypothesized that the formalism parallels Hermitian scattering. The innovation is expected to emerge via complexification of parameters. The model assumes the potential vanishes beyond a certain distance. The energy variable ϕ is constrained to a specific range. The method relies on matching boundary conditions at the cutoff. The goal is to reduce the problem to linear algebra. The study tests the applicability of matrix inversion for scattering.

Methodological Details
The study uses a one-dimensional scattering problem with a complex potential. The potential V(x) is defined as Z(x) + iY(x). Z(x) is real and even, while Y(x) is real and odd. The Schrödinger equation is discretized using the Runge-Kutta method. The lattice step h is a positive parameter. The potential is assumed to vanish for |k| ≥ M. The energy is parameterized by ϕ where 2 cos ϕ = 2 − h²E. The boundary conditions specify incoming, reflected, and transmitted waves. The conventional choice is A = 1 for the incident wave. The model is tested for cutoffs M = 1, 2, and 3. For M=1, the system degenerates to three nontrivial relations. For M=2, the system involves four known quantities. The method involves matching wavefunctions at the potential boundaries. The matrix T is a (2M − 1)-dimensional square matrix. The inverse matrix R is partitioned to extract coefficients α and β.

The difference Schrödinger equation is written as a linear system. The system matrix S_k depends on the potential and energy. The eigenvector components are prescribed by boundary conditions. The infinite system is reduced to a finite non-square matrix. This is further reduced to a non-homogeneous system of 2M − 1 equations. The matrix T is partitioned into submatrices for inversion. The inverse matrix R is decomposed into blocks α, β, Q, etc. The coefficients α and β carry the dynamical input information. β is equal to 1/det T, and α has the same denominator. Explicit determinants are calculated for M=2, M=3, and M=4. For M=2, det T involves Z0, Z1, and Y1. For M=3, the determinant includes higher-order products of couplings. For M=4, symbolic manipulations on a computer are recommended. The final coefficients B and C are solved via elimination. The transmission coefficient C is given by a specific rational formula.

The study shows a close parallelism between Hermitian and PT-symmetric scattering. The definition of transmission and reflection coefficients is identical. This approach may inform non-Hermitian inverse scattering problems. The work fills a gap in the literature on PT-symmetric scattering. The model is limited to short-range potentials. The discretization introduces O(h⁴) discrepancies. The energy is constrained to E ∈ (0, 4/h²). summary.title: Inertial Screening in Sedimentation
summary.executive_summary: This study investigates the sedimentation dynamics of semi-dilute suspensions of non-Brownian spheres across a range of Reynolds numbers (0.001 to 2.3), extending previous work from the Stokes regime into the moderately inertial regime. Using particle image velocimetry (PIV), the authors measure velocity fields and fluctuations in suspensions of glass beads with a volume fraction of 0.06. The central finding is the identification of a critical Reynolds number, Rec ≈ 0.05, where inertial effects begin to significantly alter the sedimentation dynamics. Below this threshold, the system behaves according to classical Stokes sedimentation theory, exhibiting large, Reynolds-number-independent velocity fluctuations and correlation lengths. Above Rec, inertial screening reduces both the magnitude of velocity fluctuations (σV/V) and the spatial extent of correlations (ξ). The reduction in fluctuation magnitude is substantial, reaching approximately 80% at the highest Reynolds number tested (Re = 2.3). The authors propose a modified Hinch force balance model that incorporates Reynolds-number-dependent drag coefficients to connect the fluctuation magnitudes to the correlation sizes. This model successfully predicts the observed trends across the entire studied range. The onset of inertial effects is rationalized by the equivalence of the inertial screening length (l = a/Re) and the Stokes sedimentation length (ξ0). Additionally, the study validates Brenner's criterion regarding the ratio of particle diffusion to fluid viscosity. The results reconcile previous experimental findings that reported no inertial effects at moderate Reynolds numbers by showing those experiments were conducted below the critical threshold. This work provides a crucial benchmark for theoretical models of moderately inertial sedimentation, demonstrating that inertia screens hydrodynamic interactions and modifies the statistical properties of settling particles.

The study aims to demonstrate how moderate fluid inertia affects settling dynamics. The hypothesis is that inertial corrections occur when inertial screening length matches Stokes length. It is predicted that inertial screening reduces fluctuation magnitude and spatial extent. A modified Hinch model is proposed to connect fluctuation magnitudes to correlation sizes. The onset of inertial effects occurs when inertial screening length matches Stokes length. This corresponds to Rec ≈ 0.04, agreeing with the observed 0.05. The model was tested by neglecting inertial drag corrections. This ablation showed that both ξ reduction and drag increase are important. The empirical fit for ξ was used to test the Hinch model.

Figure 1 shows PIV results for velocities and fluctuations at three Reynolds numbers. Figure 2 compares spatial correlation functions for Stokes and inertial regimes. Figure 3 shows correlation lengths and normalized fluctuations vs. Re. Figure 4 plots viscosity, diffusion coefficient, and their ratio vs. Re.

1. The core contribution is the identification of inertial screening in sedimentation at Rec ≈ 0.05. 2. Executive Summary
This paper presents RIDGE, a data analysis pipeline for triggered gravitational wave (GW) burst searches, which differ fundamentally from all-sky blind searches due to available prior information and smaller data volumes. The authors argue that triggered searches allow for computationally expensive preprocessing algorithms that are impractical for high-data-volume untriggered searches. The pipeline consists of two main stages: data conditioning and detection statistic generation. For conditioning, RIDGE employs a two-step process: first, estimating the noise floor using a running median to reject outliers like narrowband artifacts, and second, applying Finite Impulse Response (FIR) filters to whiten the data. A subsequent line estimation and removal step (MBLT) eliminates strong narrowband noise features such as power line interference. The detection statistic is based on regularized maximum likelihood, a method chosen because inverting detector responses to obtain polarization waveforms is an ill-posed problem. The authors compare two detection statistics derived from the sky-map: Rmm (ratio of max to min likelihood) and Rrad (radial distance from the mean noise location). Monte Carlo simulations using simulated LIGO and Virgo detector noise and injected sine-Gaussian signals demonstrate that Rrad outperforms Rmm. Specifically, for a signal with hrss = 5 × 10^-22 Hz^-1/2, the pipeline achieves a detection probability of approximately 62% at a false alarm probability of 10^-2. The study concludes that RIDGE provides an independent check for other pipelines and serves as a platform for testing new regulators, with future work aimed at integrating waveform estimation methods to extract astrophysical information.

Research Context
Triggered searches differ from all-sky searches due to available prior information. Prior information includes sky location and source distance. Small data volumes allow computationally expensive algorithms. Untriggered searches are limited by finite computational resources. Previous work on prior information was limited to specific events. The SGR-1806-20 search used X-ray intensity oscillations. Bayesian approaches for known pulsars are a model for future work.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The study aims to describe a data analysis pipeline for triggered searches. The pipeline is named RIDGE and uses new algorithms. The hypothesis is that reduced parameter space increases sensitivity. The study tests if computationally expensive preprocessing improves results. The goal is to incorporate astrophysical prior information mathematically. The authors predict that full sky-map statistics are required. The study evaluates the performance of regularized maximum likelihood.

Methodological Details
The network consists of LIGO and Virgo detectors. Specific detectors used are H1, H2, L1, and V1. Simulated noise approximates LIGO SRD curves for 4km detectors. Noise was generated by filtering white noise with FIR filters. Instrumental artifacts were simulated using sinusoids at specific frequencies. Artifact frequencies included 54, 60, 120, 180, 344, 349, 407 Hz. Injected signals were sine-Gaussian with center frequency 235 Hz. The quality factor Q for the signals was 9. Signal strength was specified using hrss values. Test hrss values were 3, 5, and 7 times 10^-22. Data was sampled at 16384 Hz. Integration time for sky-map generation was 0.5 seconds. The source location was set to GRB060813 coordinates.

Procedures And Architectures
Data conditioning starts with estimating the noise floor. A running median is used to estimate the PSD. The running median rejects outliers like narrowband noise. A digital filter whitens the data using the PSD. Whitening filters are Finite Impulse Response (FIR) filters. Filter coefficients are obtained from a training data segment. Line estimation and removal uses the MBLT method. MBLT estimates amplitude and phase modulation of line features. The detection statistic uses regularized maximum likelihood. The problem of inverting detector responses is ill-posed. Regularization is required to solve the inversion problem. The specific regularization scheme was developed in reference 10. The output is a sky-map S(theta, phi). Two statistics are compared: Rmm and Rrad. Rmm is the ratio of max to min likelihood. Rrad is the radial distance from the mean noise location.

Key Results
Rrad performs better than Rmm in ROC curves. An hrss of 5 × 10^-22 Hz^-1/2 is detectable. Detection probability is approximately 62% for this signal. False alarm probability is 10^-2. False alarm rate corresponds to 1 event in 50 seconds. The pipeline provides an independent check for other pipelines. Line removal does not significantly affect transient signals. The running median rejects transient signals as outliers. The sky-map rings off the entire sky for signals. The integration time of 0.5 sec is a lower bound.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
Triggered searches benefit from reduced parameter space search volume. Using full sky-map information is crucial for sensitivity. Regularization is necessary due to the ill-posed nature of inversion. The hard constraint algorithm is a limit of the regulator. RIDGE serves as a platform for testing new regulators. Future work will integrate waveform estimation methods. The pipeline can reconstruct h+ and h× waveforms.

Contradictions And Limitations
Non-stationarity in noise floor can create filter discrepancies. Concrete work on handling non-stationarity is lacking in GW literature. The 0.5 sec integration time limits performance estimates. Filter delays are currently not removed in the pipeline. The study uses simulated data, not real detector data. The source location is fixed to a specific trigger.

Claims
RIDGE pipeline is sensitive to triggered gravitational wave bursts. Detection probability is 62% for hrss 5e-22. False alarm probability is 10^-2. Performance estimates are lower bounds due to integration time. RIDGE provides an independent check for other pipelines.
Rrad statistic outperforms Rmm statistic. ROC curves show Rrad performs better.  Full sky-map statistics are required for triggered searches.

Data And Code Availability
The code for the pipeline is called RIDGE. The code is written mostly in matlab. The paper does not describe the code in detail.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
Running median rejects outliers in PSD estimation. MBLT line removal does not affect transient signals. Filter delays are a known limitation.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1 shows PSD and running median estimate. Figure 2 shows spectrograms before and after line removal. Figure 3 shows sky-maps for noise and signal cases. Figure 4 shows PSDs of simulated detector noise. Figure 5 shows detector responses to injection signal. Figure 6 shows ROC curves for Rmm and Rrad.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is the RIDGE pipeline for triggered searches. 2. The strongest evidence is the 62% detection probability for hrss 5e-22. 3. The future path is integrating waveform estimation methods.
